1. Key Takeaways

The analysis investigated how kangaroo species are classified by their skull features. We looked at three species here: fuliginosus, giganteus, and melanops, and analyzed a sample of 148 individual kangaroos, distinguished by sex and skull measurements. Our findings suggest that skull features provide useful information for identifying species, however, some species are more difficult to distinguish than others.

Before attempting to classify, we built 3 exploratory plots. For example, Figure 3 shows the distribution of zygomatic width in male and female kangaroos across the three species. The distribution overlap suggested that this measurement alone doesn’t do a good job at distinguishing all three species.

Figure 4 illustrates a decision tree, or a model that makes predictions by dividing observations into homogenous groups based on skull measurements. However, we used the forest algorithm which is a method that combines predictions from many decision trees, each using different subsets measurements, to make a more reliable final prediction. A random forest achieved an approximate of 75.25% accuracy. It was derived from out-of-bag predictions(where each decision tree was tested using skull features that were left out when an individual tree was built), providing estimates of how well our model will classify new kangaroos. Model accuracy was significantly higher than the 34% accuracy from simply guessing the most common species. The model correctly classified 49 out of 50 M. Fuliginosus skulls in predictions based on training data, but had challenges distinguishing M.giganteus from M.melanops. Moreover, when trying to identify most useful predictors, we determined that nasal length, crest width, and zygomatic width are the most influential measurements in distinguishing species, which is evident from Figure 5. Sex contributed the least.

The results should be implemented with caution since we were limited by a relatively small sample size of 101 skull measurements, after removing 47 observations missing the measurements. Since its settings were not extensively optimized and its accuracy was estimated using the given data, testing it on a larger, independent dataset would determine how reliably it can classify unfamiliar specimens. Moreover, many skull measurements are strongly correlated, meaning they might capture similar aspects of skull size rather than distinct characteristics. The model also assumes that future skulls will have similar measurement patterns to those in our dataset.





2. Technical details

Most of skull measurements are strongly correlated, since they largely reflect overall skull size. (i included that in our limitations so no need to include it here ig)

# Plot 1: Predictors used (1): nasal.length
ggplot(kangaroos, aes(x = species, y = nasal.length, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Nasal Length Distributions Across Species",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Nasal Length (mm)",
    caption = "Figure 1"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") 
# Plot 2: Predictors used (2): crest.width & mandible.width
ggplot(kangaroos, aes(x = crest.width, y = mandible.width, color = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, position = "jitter") +
  labs(
    title = "Crest Width by Mandible Width",
    x = "Crest Width(mm)",
    y = "Mandible Width(mm)",
    caption = "Figure 2"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
# Plot 3: Predictors used (2): zygomatic.width & sex
  ggplot(kangaroos, aes(x = zygomatic.width, fill = species)) + 
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) + 
  facet_wrap("sex") +
  labs(
    title = "Species by Zygomatic Width Faceted by Sex",
    x = "Zygomatic Width(mm)",
    y = "Density",
    caption = "Figure 3"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

A single deep classification tree would therefore depend heavily on which of several nearly interchangeable measurements it happened to split on, which makes it unstable and prone to overfitting. We used a random forest instead. Averaging many decorrelated trees reduces that variance, and the forest still lets us rank which measurements matter most.

# STEP 1: tree specification with specific tuning parameter values

tree_spec <- decision_tree() |>
  set_mode("classification") |> 
  set_engine(engine = "rpart") |> 
  set_args(cost_complexity = 0, min_n = 2, tree_depth = 30)

# STEP 2: Build the tree!
# Note that we specified our tuning parameters in Step 1.
# Thus no tuning (hence no workflows) necessary.
kangaroo_tree <- tree_spec |> 
  fit(species ~ ., data = kangaroos)

# Plot the tree
kangaroo_tree |> 
  extract_fit_engine() |> 
  plot(margin = 0) 
kangaroo_tree |> 
  extract_fit_engine() |> 
  text(cex = 0.7)

Species was treated as a categorical response, with all 19 other variables as predictors. Of the 148 skulls, 47 were missing at least one measurement and were dropped, leaving 101 complete cases. We grew 500 classification trees, each on a bootstrap sample of those 101 skulls. At each split, 4 of the 19 predictors were randomly chosen as candidates, and the split minimising Gini impurity was chosen. Trees were grown deep, with a minimum node size of 2, and each skull’s class is the majority vote across trees. These were default settings and were not tuned. We set the random seed to 253.

# There's randomness behind the splits!

set.seed(253)
    
# STEP 1: Model Specification
rf_spec <- rand_forest()  |>
  set_mode("classification") |>
  set_engine(engine = "ranger") |> 
  set_args(
    mtry = NULL,
    trees = 500,
    min_n = 2,
    probability = FALSE,    # Report classifications, not probability calculations
    importance = "impurity" # Use Gini index to measure variable importance
  )
    
# STEP 2: Build the forest
# There are no preprocessing steps or tuning, hence no need for a workflow!
kangaroo_forest <- rf_spec |> 
  fit(species ~ ., data = kangaroos)

kangaroo_forest

## OOB prediction error:             24.75 %

We estimated performance with out-of-bag (OOB) error: each skull is classified using only the one-third of trees whose bootstrap samples left it out. The OOB error was 24.75%, so we expect about 75.25% of new skulls to be classified correctly. Guessing the most common species would get about 34% right (where is this from??)

# The cbind() includes the original candy data
# alongside their predicted popularity levels
kangaroo_forest |> 
  predict(new_data = kangaroos) |> 
  cbind(kangaroos) |> 
  conf_mat(
    truth = species,
    estimate = .pred_class
  )
##              Truth
## Prediction    fuliginosus giganteus melanops
##   fuliginosus          49         1        2
##   giganteus             1        42       11
##   melanops              0         7       35
#Overall accuracy
(49+42+35)/148
## [1] 0.8513514

The confusion matrix shows a clear pattern in the errors. Fuliginosus is almost always identified correctly (49 of 50). Nearly all misclassifications are between giganteus and melanops: 11 melanops skulls were labelled giganteus, and 7 giganteus skulls were labelled melanops. Even when predicting its own training data, the forest cannot fully separate these two species, which points to real overlap in their skull measurements.

# Print the metrics
kangaroo_forest |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  pluck("variable.importance") |> 
  sort(decreasing = TRUE)

# Plot the metrics
library(vip)
kangaroo_forest |> 
  vip(geom = "point", num_features = 20)

Variable importance, measured by the total decrease in Gini impurity, ranks nasal length, crest width, and zygomatic width highest, followed by mandible width and nasal width. Sex contributes almost nothing. Figures 1–3 show how these top predictors are distributed across species.
